title: The friction surface lab
subtitle: Summer 2 • Choose a surface using controlled evidence
objective: Compare a sliding block’s movement on different surfaces and explain the effect of friction using a controlled test.

sow.exactOutcome: Compare how things move on different surfaces; explore friction (push and pull).
sow.alignment: Chronological continuation of the supplied SOW. This lesson develops or reviews the named outcome; it does not claim an accreditation award.

priorLearning: A push or pull can change movement.
A comparison needs a consistent measurement rule.
success: Describe friction opposing this block’s sliding.
Name the changed surface and important controls.

vocabulary.meaning: A contact force that opposes sliding between surfaces.
The outside layer in contact with an object.
Distance travelled along the level test surface after leaving the ramp.
A comparison with relevant conditions kept the same.

equipment: Printed shared evidence and one chosen pupil route; pencil; optional ruler; projector or offline HTML.
Optional low stable ramp with a smooth flush transition to a tabletop tray; small wooden sliding block; card, cloth and rubber test strips; ruler; barrier to catch the block.
preparation: Print the shared evidence, one response route and exit page. Routes are alternatives, not a workload ladder.
Read the worked answers. Prepare an oral, pointing or adult-scribed route where useful.

Adult pilots a low ramp so the block slides without tumbling or snagging and stops within the tray. Fix the ramp and transition; use the same block/contact face and marked release point without a push.

The supplied constructed distances allow the full lesson without equipment. For real trials measure from the ramp end to the same trailing block edge at stopping; use three releases per surface and keep actual results separate.
safety: Keep the activity on a stable table in a contained tray with a stop barrier. No pupils sliding on floors or ramps.
Use a small block, low ramp and clear release area; keep hands out of its path. No heavy falling objects or stretched elastic launchers.
Do not lubricate the surfaces or create a floor-slip hazard. Stop any setup that tips, snags or lets the block leave the tray.
practicalAlternative: All core reasoning uses the supplied evidence and can be completed in 40 minutes without a live practical.

misconceptions.correction: Friction can provide useful grip or slow sliding; usefulness depends on the purpose.
misconceptions.check: Ask whether a surface should stop or allow the block to slide.

misconceptions.claim: The surface with the longest run-out has the most slowing effect.
misconceptions.correction: Under the same release conditions, greater resistance usually reduces run-out.

misconceptions.claim: A smooth-looking material always has least friction.
misconceptions.correction: Friction depends on the pair of materials and conditions; appearance alone is insufficient.
misconceptions.check: Ask for test evidence rather than a universal texture rule.

access.supported: Short choices, word bank and pointing or adult-scribed reasons; same core scientific goal.
access.standard: Make a short evidence-based explanation or record using the supplied information.
access.stretch: Apply the core idea to a changed case, evaluate evidence or identify a limit.
access.regulation: Preview the sequence. Offer seated observation, quiet paired rehearsal, private feedback and a pass from public sharing. Routes respond to current access needs, not a diagnosis.

slides.title: Which surface should stop the sliding block sooner?
slides.notes: Set purpose: choose a surface for a small model stopping zone, not for real vehicle safety equipment.

slides.title: Retrieve pushes, pulls and comparisons
body: 2. Name one thing to keep the same in a test.
3. What unit can measure a short distance?
slides.notes: 1 motion/speed/direction. 2 relevant control accepted. 3 cm. Explain that a block already moving can continue after a hand stops pushing.

slides.title: I distinguish motion from force
slides.notes: Think aloud: “The direction of movement is not automatically the direction of every force. Here friction opposes the sliding and slows the unpushed block.” This is not a complete force diagram: weight and support act vertically.

visual.title: Friction opposes sliding at the contact
visual.description: A wooden block is already sliding to the right on a stationary horizontal surface after leaving a ramp. Friction on the block points left. The movement arrow is distinct from a force arrow; vertical forces are omitted from this simplified focus diagram.

elements.text: After release: no hand keeps pushing the block.

slides.title: I keep the start conditions fixed
slides.notes: Shares I do time. Think aloud: “A higher release might travel further even on the same material. I keep the ramp and release fixed before comparing surfaces.” Fix surface strips flat with comparable transitions and no bunching.

visual.title: Change the horizontal test surface only
visual.description: Side-view fixed ramp feeds a sliding wooden block onto a horizontal test surface. The same block is released without a push from one marked point; ramp angle, release point, transition and block face stay fixed. Run-out is measured from the ramp end to the same chosen block edge when stopped.

elements.text: Use the same trailing edge at ramp end and when stopped.

slides.title: I use repeats before choosing
body: A longer run-out means less slowing here.
slides.notes: Shares I do time. Think aloud: “Card is around 60 cm, rubber around 15 cm. In this setup rubber gives shorter run-out. I do not claim the material name gives the same result with every object.” Means are supplied summaries; core pupils can compare repeated ranges.

visual.title: Compare distance after the same release
visual.description: Horizontal bars start at zero and show constructed means: card 60 cm, cloth 23 cm, rubber 15 cm. They summarise three supplied repeated runs on each surface, not universal material constants.

slides.title: The surface-selection meeting
body: Use two readings in your reason.
slides.notes: W1: rubber gives shortest run-out (14–16 cm). Partners take client and evidence adviser roles; client challenges a claim with a table reading.

table.caption: Constructed sliding-block data; same ramp, block face and release

slides.title: Repair a changed release
body: A team pushes only the rubber run.
slides.notes: W2: no; a push changes initial conditions. Repeat using the same marked release without a push; retain/annotate the flawed run rather than silently replacing it.
slides.reveal: Use comparable starts and record any method change.

slides.title: The block slides right after release.
body: Which friction statement fits this setup?
slides.notes: Correct first option. If second chosen, point to relative sliding at the contact.

options.text: Friction on the block acts left, opposing sliding.
options.feedback: It opposes relative sliding on the stationary surface.

options.text: Friction acts right because the block moves right.
options.feedback: Movement and friction point in opposite directions here.

options.text: No force can affect the block after the hand lets go.
options.feedback: Contact friction can continue after release.

slides.title: Choose your science route
body: Review the strength of the test.
slides.notes: Set ONE route. Use supplied readings for the core task; optional practical after adult setup check. Keep actual values separately labelled. Do not require forces equations, coefficients or mean calculation for BUILD.

slides.title: Make your own evidence record
slides.notes: Use supplied readings for the core task; optional practical after adult setup check. Keep actual values separately labelled. Do not require forces equations, coefficients or mean calculation for BUILD.

slides.title: Check what the evidence can show
body: Point to the clue you used.
slides.notes: Shares independent time. Ask for a reason, not just a correct word. Use supplied readings for the core task; optional practical after adult setup check. Keep actual values separately labelled. Do not require forces equations, coefficients or mean calculation for BUILD.

slides.title: Lundy loop: improve the shared account
slides.notes: Listen to a selected pupil revision and visibly adopt a scientifically accurate contribution. Offer private, written or partner feedback.
slides.prompt: What made our surface choice defensible?
slides.reveal: Comparable starts, repeated distances and a purpose-specific claim make the choice stronger.

slides.title: Keep the useful change
slides.notes: Shares review time. Name how a pupil contribution changed a label, method or conclusion. Do not rank pupils.
slides.reveal: Comparable starts, repeated distances and a purpose-specific claim make the choice stronger.

pupilPages.title: Shared evidence • Constructed surface test
pupilPages.intro: Same small wooden block and contact face; fixed low ramp and release mark; no push. Only the level test surface changes. Measure from ramp end to the same trailing block edge at stopping.

blocks.text: Mean run-out: card 60 cm; cloth 23 cm; rubber 15 cm. These are summaries of supplied teaching data, not universal properties of every material pair. Friction opposes this block’s sliding.

blocks.prompt: W1. Which surface best fits a short model stopping zone? Use evidence.
W2. Why must we repair a run given an extra push?

pupilPages.title: Route 1 • Choose using the readings
pupilPages.intro: Word bank: rubber / card / same / opposite / cm.

blocks.prompt: S1. The shortest run-out is on...
S2. Give one reading supporting your choice.
S3. The block slides right. Friction on it acts...
S4. Name two things the fair test keeps the same.
S5. Would you give one run an extra push? Why?

pupilPages.title: Route 2 • Write a surface recommendation
pupilPages.intro: Recommend a material for this model stopping zone, using repeated evidence.

blocks.prompt: M1. State the changed factor and measured outcome.
M2. Compare card and rubber using their repeated ranges.
M3. Explain friction’s direction and effect after release.
M4. Write a short method with a consistent release, distance rule and repeat.

pupilPages.title: Route 3 • Review the test quality
pupilPages.intro: A designer claims: “Rubber always has the most friction, so our result proves the safest surface for every purpose.”

blocks.prompt: T1. Limit the claim to the actual object and setup.
T2. Explain why a different material pair or condition could need a new test.
T3. A model needs a long sliding distance instead. Which supplied surface fits that purpose?
T4. One cloth strip bunches up and stops the block. How should the team record and investigate this?

pupilPages.intro: Point, draw, write or tell an adult.

answers.label: We do W1–W2
answers.answer: W1 rubber, 14–16 cm compared with card 58–62 cm and cloth 22–24 cm; it fits shorter run-out here. W2 an extra push changes starting conditions; repeat from the same release mark without a push and annotate the flawed run.

answers.label: Hinge
answers.answer: First option correct. Friction on the right-sliding block points left; contact force persists after release.

answers.label: S1–S5
answers.answer: S1 rubber. S2 14,15 or16 cm. S3 left. S4 same block/contact face, ramp/release point, transition, distance rule or other relevant condition. S5 no: changes start conditions.

answers.label: M1–M4
answers.answer: M1 change horizontal surface; measure run-out distance in cm. M2 card 58–62 cm; rubber 14–16 cm, rubber shorter in every run. M3 friction opposes relative sliding, acts left on right-moving block and slows it after release. M4 fix ramp and mark; same block/face; release without push; measure from ramp end to same trailing edge at rest; repeat three runs per surface and retain records.

answers.label: T1–T4
answers.answer: T1 rubber gave the shortest run-out for this wooden block/contact face and controlled setup. T2 friction depends on the pair, surface condition and loading; a different use needs relevant evidence. T3 card, about 60 cm here. T4 record the bunching/snag and affected run, secure the strip flat with comparable transition, repeat under the stated method and distinguish snagging from normal sliding resistance.

answers.label: Exit E1–E3
answers.answer: E1 relative sliding between block and surface. E2 rubber. E3 fixed ramp angle/release mark, same block face, no push or comparable transition.

answers.label: R1–R2
answers.answer: Responses vary. Credit a scientific revision, evidence-based defence or relevant next question. A private or oral response has equal value.

teacherNotes: 40 minutes: opening 2, retrieval 3, I do 7, We do 8, hinge 3, independent 12, review 3, exit 2. Zero-minute slides share the named stage time.
BUILD uses the supplied Year 3 science anchor with age-respectful contexts for older pupils. Supported, standard and stretch are selectable routes within the pathway.

Interactive We do: predict first, test against the controlled SVG model or supplied evidence, then explain or revise. Shared W tasks offer the equivalent paper discussion. Animation is a teaching representation, not filmed experimental evidence.
Keep constructed evidence separate from actual class observations. Do not invent measurements or require internet research.
Horizontal run-out is a comparison of slowing in this apparatus, not a direct coefficient-of-friction measurement. Ramp losses and initial conditions must remain comparable.
Secure core: correct friction direction for this setup, table-supported comparison and one meaningful control. The lesson does not recommend surfaces for real safety-critical equipment.
